subject: design
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Coverage, Philosophy of the skill, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and established usability practice (think-aloud protocol, Nielsen/Landauer 5-user rule, Nielsen 0-4 severity scale, formative vs summative testing, SUS).

cases.scenario: A stakeholder wants to run a 5-user test and use the results to claim the redesign improved task success rate by a statistically significant margin over the old design.
cases.context: The claim will be presented to leadership as a benchmark comparison.
cases.question: How should the agent respond to this plan?
expected_flags: The 5-user rule applies to formative diagnostic testing, not summative/benchmark claims
A statistical success-rate comparison needs a much larger sample
5 users surfaces ~85% of major problems per segment/task — it does not establish significance
Conflating formative and summative purposes invalidates the claim
expected_fix_hints: Use 5 users to find issues formatively; size a separate larger study for the benchmark claim
Reframe the leadership message as diagnostic findings, not a statistical win
absent_signals: Do not present 5-user results as statistical proof
Do not apply the 5-user rule to a summative comparison

cases.scenario: A draft test script tells participants 'Click the Tax Summary tab, then click View Details to see what you owe this quarter.'
cases.context: The team wants to know whether users can find their quarterly tax owed.
cases.question: How should the agent revise the task?
expected_flags: Tasks must be written as goals, not step-by-step instructions
Prescribing the steps tests obedience, not discoverability
Rewrite as a goal: 'find out how much you owe in taxes this quarter'
A participant should be able to attempt the task without being shown the path
expected_fix_hints: Convert each instruction-style task into a goal-framed scenario
Remove UI element names from the task wording
absent_signals: Do not name the tabs/buttons to click in the task
Do not lead the participant to the intended path

cases.scenario: During a session, a participant gets stuck on a step and the moderator immediately explains how the feature 'is supposed to work' so the participant can continue.
cases.context: The moderator wants the participant to finish all tasks.
cases.question: What should the agent flag about the moderation?
expected_flags: Explaining the design after a participant gets stuck destroys the evidence
The obstacle the participant hit is the finding and cannot be re-observed in that session
The moderator's job is to stay neutral, let silence/struggle sit, and not rescue or defend
Most common moderator utterances should be open questions ('what are you thinking?') and silence
expected_fix_hints: Coach the moderator to let the participant struggle and observe, not explain
Capture the obstacle as a finding rather than coaching past it
absent_signals: Do not have the moderator explain or defend the design mid-task
Do not prioritize task completion over preserving the obstacle

cases.scenario: A test produced 14 findings presented as an unranked flat list, treating a label typo and a checkout-blocking dead end as equally important.
cases.context: The team has limited time before the next release and must triage.
cases.question: How should the agent organize the findings?
expected_flags: Rate findings by Nielsen's 0-4 severity scale (cosmetic / minor / major / catastrophic)
A catastrophic blocker must be distinguishable from a cosmetic issue
Severity enables triage under time pressure
Listing findings flat hides what actually must be fixed first
expected_fix_hints: Assign a 0-4 severity to each finding
Sort the catastrophic/major issues to the top of the fix list
absent_signals: Do not present findings as an unranked flat list

cases.scenario: A team must choose between a moderated study with 6 scheduled sessions and an unmoderated tool that can run 40 sessions this week, for an early prototype with a novel interaction they don't fully understand yet.
cases.context: The interaction is new and the team expects surprising behavior they'd want to probe.
cases.question: Which approach should the agent recommend and why?
expected_flags: Moderated gives richer data and the ability to follow up on surprises; costs more and needs scheduling
Unmoderated is cheaper and scales but sacrifices follow-up on surprises
Because the interaction is novel and surprises are expected, lean moderated to probe the unexpected
Matches method choice to whether probing surprises or volume matters more
expected_fix_hints: Prefer moderated for the novel interaction; consider unmoderated later for volume validation
Reserve follow-up probing for the riskiest unknowns
absent_signals: Do not pick unmoderated purely for volume when probing surprises is the point

cases.scenario: A test report says every participant completed every task smoothly and the design was confirmed entirely, with no obstacles found.
cases.context: The team is ready to declare the design validated.
cases.question: How should the agent interpret a fully-confirming result?
expected_flags: A session that confirms the design entirely is suspect
Likely the tasks were too easy or the moderator was unintentionally helping
Recommends checking whether any finding contradicted a prior expectation
Suggests harder/goal-framed tasks and neutral moderation before declaring validation
expected_fix_hints: Audit the task difficulty and moderator neutrality
Re-run with harder, goal-framed tasks to surface real obstacles
absent_signals: Do not treat an all-confirming result as proof the design works

cases.scenario: An engineer asks the usability-testing owner to 'set up our usability tests in CI' meaning unit and integration tests, and a load test against the checkout API.
cases.context: The shared word 'test' has caused the team to route this to usability testing.
cases.question: How should the agent scope the request?
expected_flags: Automated unit/integration tests and load tests are out of scope — that is testing-strategy
Usability testing is empirical observation of real humans attempting tasks, not engineering verification
The shared word 'test' hides two unrelated activities
Correctly redirects to testing-strategy rather than answering out of lane
expected_fix_hints: Offer in-scope help only if the team wants to observe real users on the checkout flow
absent_signals: Do not treat CI/automated tests as usability testing
Do not author unit or load tests under the usability banner
